item.research_question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?
item.material_system: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at% W, 20 at% Ta, 20 at% Mo, 20 at% Nb, 20 at% V)
item.processing_route: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system with 400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere, mixed elemental powders (20-70 µm, irregular shape) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; parameters: laser power 160–244 W, spot size 80 µm, scanning speed 300–700 mm/s, hatch spacing 0.10–0.12 mm, layer thickness 0.3 mm, energy density 38.1–162.7 J/mm³; rotation of 67° per layer. Reference sample produced by Arc Melting Furnace (AMF) with 12 g mixed powder compacted to 50% green density.
item.test_conditions: Microstructure: SEM, TEM (200 kV), XRD (CuKα, 40 kV/30 mA, 2°/min). Physical: Vickers hardness, compression strength (0.5 mm/min crosshead speed). Electrochemical: Potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl at ambient temperature (0.5 mV/s scan rate, SCE reference).
key_findings: Both LPBF and AMF samples formed a single solid phase solution with a BCC crystal structure and a lattice parameter of 3.2 Å.
LPBF samples exhibited a finer average grain size of 10 µm compared to 25 µm for AMF samples.
LPBF samples achieved a maximum density of 95% in advanced trials, compared to 38% in primary trials.
The ultimate compressive strength of the LPBF sample was slightly higher than that of the AMF counterpart.
LPBF samples showed a maximum crack density of 6.4×10⁻⁷ μm⁻².
Sub-grains of approximately 500 nm and high-density dislocations were observed in the LPBF matrix via TEM.
Spherical precipitates of 60–80 nm containing 33 at% V and 7.9 at% W were found at intergranular boundaries in LPBF samples.
Both alloys demonstrated excellent corrosion resistance with an active-passive transition mode in 3.5% NaCl solution.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the distribution of elements to melting temperature differences, noting that vanadium's lower melting point (1910 °C) causes it to solidify at grain boundaries during the final stage, while tungsten's high melting point (3422 °C) and density lead to segregation. The finer grain size and higher strength in LPBF are attributed to rapid solidification characteristics and inherent internal stresses generating dislocations. The presence of precipitates and elemental segregation is linked to the end-stage solidification dynamics and the irregular shape of the mixed elemental powders affecting laser interaction.
item.limitations: The authors state that the LPBF process resulted in inherent printing defects such as lack-of-fusion, porosity, and unmelted powder particles, which induced brittleness. They also note that the passivation stability of the LPBF alloy was reduced due to increased surface roughness, leading to current density fluctuations and a higher number of small pits compared to the AMF alloy.
item.future_work: The authors propose that additional experimental work is required to further optimize printing parameters to obtain improved properties and microstructure characteristics, specifically to reduce printing defects. They also suggest including post-heat treatments to upgrade the homogeneity of the LPBF alloy and its synthesis characteristics.
quotes: The results disclosed similarities in microstructure, physical properties and electrochemical behavior between HEA WTaMoNbV manufactured by the proposed LPBF process and its counterpart alloy produced by an AMF process.
This can be attributed mainly to the relatively high melting temperature and high density of W compared to other alloying elements.
Further experimental work is needed to continue to optimize the printing parameters of the LPBF process along with possible a post-heat-treatment process to rectify inherent printing defects.
